unit-m3u2.title: Unit 3 · Lesson 2: Estimate Products
unit-m3u2.source: enVision Topic 3 textbook scan — Multiply Multi-Digit Whole Numbers (Drive)

summary.text: Lesson 3-2 of the Topic 3 textbook scan: estimating products by rounding and with compatible numbers, and deciding whether an estimate is an overestimate or an underestimate.

why.text: Estimating is how she will check every multiplication in the rest of this unit — and it is often the whole answer when a question only asks "is it enough?"

objectives.text: Tell whether an estimate is an overestimate or an underestimate
Choose an underestimate to prove "at least"

parentNote.text: The idea most worth a word is which way an estimate is off. Rounding both factors up gives an overestimate, both down gives an underestimate, and one of each gives no promise at all — one question shows 48 × 52 estimated as 2,500 when the real answer is 2,496, just under. The other idea is choosing the right kind of estimate: to PROVE there is at least enough of something, only an underestimate that clears the bar does the job. That is lv3 and one question is built around it.

nextUp.text: Round, multiply, then ask: is my estimate too big or too small?

cards.def:
**Round each factor to a friendly number, then multiply those.**
• 38 × 612 → 40 × 600 = 24,000.
• An estimate tells you roughly how big the answer should be.
cards.hint: Round, then use your powers-of-10 patterns.

cards.def:
**Numbers that are easy to multiply in your head, like 25 and 4.**
• 25 × 4 = 100, so 25 × 400 = 10,000.
• They can give a closer estimate than plain rounding.
cards.hint: Look for pairs that make 100 or 1,000.

cards.def:
**If you rounded both factors UP, your estimate is more than the real answer.**
• 29 × 488 → 30 × 500 = 15,000, which is too high.
cards.hint: Rounded up → answer came out too big.

cards.def:
**If you rounded both factors DOWN, your estimate is less than the real answer.**
• 41 × 207 → 40 × 200 = 8,000, which is too low.
cards.hint: Rounded down → answer came out too small.

cards.def:
**If one factor went up and the other went down, you cannot tell which way the estimate is off.**
• 48 × 52 → 50 × 50 = 2,500, but the real answer is 2,496.
cards.hint: Up and down together — no promise either way.

cards.def:
**To prove you have AT LEAST enough, use an underestimate.**
• If even the too-small estimate is enough, the real amount is too.
cards.hint: An underestimate that clears the bar proves it.

questions.q: Round each factor to its greatest place. What is the estimate for 38 × 612?
questions.hint: 38 rounds to 40. What does 612 round to?

ex.main: **24,000.** 40 × 600 is 4 × 6 = 24 with three zeros on the end.
ex.tip: 2,400 has one zero too few — both 40 and 600 bring zeros.

questions.q: Rounding 29 × 488 to 30 × 500 gives which kind of estimate?
opts: An underestimate, because both numbers were rounded up
An overestimate, because both numbers were rounded up
An overestimate, because the answer is a large number
An exact answer, because the rounding was careful
questions.hint: Did 29 and 488 get bigger or smaller when you rounded them?
steps: Both factors got bigger, so the estimate is bigger than the real product.

ex.main: **An overestimate.** Both factors were rounded up, so the estimate comes out too high.
ex.tip: Whether it is over or under depends on the direction of rounding, not on the size of the answer.

questions.hint: 26 is close to 25, and 397 is close to 400.
steps: Use 25 in place of 26 and 400 in place of 397.

ex.main: **10,000.** 25 and 400 are compatible because 25 × 4 = 100 is easy in your head.
ex.tip: 8,000 comes from rounding 26 all the way down to 20 — further off than it needs to be.

questions.hint: Round each factor to its greatest place.

ex.main: **35,000.** 50 × 700 is 35 with the three zeros from 50 and 700.
ex.tip: 3,500 is what you get if you forget the zero that 50 brings.

questions.q: Which is the most reasonable estimate for 21 × 305?
steps: The real product, 6,405, is close to 6,000.

ex.main: **6,000.** 20 × 300 lands close to the real product of 6,405.
ex.tip: 600 and 60,000 are each off by a whole power of 10 — a zero was lost or added.

questions.q: Is 8,000 an overestimate or an underestimate for 41 × 207?
opts: An overestimate, because both numbers were rounded down
An underestimate, because both numbers were rounded down
An underestimate, because 8,000 ends in zeros
Neither, because 8,000 is the exact product
questions.hint: What happened to 41 and 207 when they became 40 and 200?
steps: Both factors got smaller, so the estimate is smaller than the real product (8,487).

ex.main: **An underestimate.** Both factors were rounded down, so 8,000 is less than the real 8,487.
ex.tip: Rounded down means the estimate sits below the true answer.

questions.q: A bake sale needs at least $2,000. It sells 48 trays at $52 each. Which estimate PROVES it reached $2,000?
opts: 50 × 50 = 2,500, because it is the closest estimate
50 × 60 = 3,000, because it is the biggest estimate
40 × 50 = 2,000, because both numbers were rounded down
48 × 50 = 2,400, because 48 was not rounded at all
questions.hint: An estimate proves "at least" only if it is too SMALL and still reaches the goal.
steps: 40 × 50 rounds both factors down, so it is an underestimate.
So the real total must be at least $2,000 too.
50 × 50 rounds one factor up and one down, so it proves nothing either way.

ex.main: **40 × 50 = 2,000.** It is an underestimate that still reaches the goal, so the real total (48 × 52 = 2,496) must reach it too.
ex.tip: A bigger estimate can feel more reassuring, but only an underestimate can prove "at least".

questions.q: Which is NOT a reasonable estimate for 32 × 289?
questions.hint: The real product is a little over 9,000. Which option is far away from that?
steps: 6,000 comes from rounding 289 down to 200, which is far too low.

ex.main: **6,000.** It rounds 289 down to 200, even though 289 is much closer to 300.
ex.tip: Round to the NEAREST hundred — 289 is 11 away from 300 but 89 away from 200.

questions.q: Kai estimates 24 × 386 as 20 × 400. Lena estimates it as 25 × 400. Whose estimate is closer to the real product?
opts: Lena's, because 25 is much closer to 24 than 20 is
Kai's, because rounding to tens is always closer
Kai's, because 8,000 is a smaller number
They are equally close, because both used 400
questions.hint: Compare how far 20 and 25 each are from 24.
steps: 10,000 is 736 away; 8,000 is 1,264 away. Lena's is closer.

ex.main: **Lena's.** Moving 24 to 25 changes it by 1; moving it to 20 changes it by 4, so her estimate stays nearer.
ex.tip: Compatible numbers are often the better choice when a factor sits right next to a friendly one.

questions.q: A factory packs 208 boxes with 12 crayons in each. Which statement is true?
opts: There are fewer than 2,000 crayons, since 12 × 200 is only 2,400
There are more than 2,000 crayons, since 12 × 200 is already 2,400
There are exactly 2,400 crayons, since 208 rounds to 200
There are fewer than 1,000 crayons, since 12 is a small number
questions.hint: 200 is less than 208, so 12 × 200 is an underestimate.
steps: That is an underestimate, and it is already more than 2,000.
So the real total (2,496) is more than 2,000.

ex.main: **More than 2,000.** 12 × 200 = 2,400 is too small an estimate and it still beats 2,000.
ex.tip: An underestimate that already clears the target settles the question without any exact math.
